I think I approached this film with the wrong expectations. I started watching it as a conventional mystery, and when almost nothing seemed to happen for quite a while, I found myself getting confused. Then, when the greenhouse came into the story, I realized that this was essentially Haruki Murakami’s “Barn Burning,” a story I had read a long time ago. From that point on, I shifted my perspective and watched it as a story in which ambiguity itself is the subject. The film scatters motifs such as plastic surgery, pantomime, cats, wells, and silent phone calls—things whose very existence becomes ambiguous as the point of view shifts. It leaves you feeling as though you’ve been told something profound, but in the end, I was left with an unsatisfying feeling of having been led down the garden path.

Burning is so so beautiful but I’m not sure if the film actually manages to say anything. If it does, it manages to say very little. The audience is consistently pointed to themes of socioeconomic divide, class resentment, male insecurity, social alienation, etc, (none of which are new or novel) but these concepts are never truly explored. The films prefers to evoke the atmosphere of these ideas rather than interrogating them (the latter being significantly harder). I’m frustrated because there’s a difference between ambiguity that generates meaning and ambiguity that withholds meaning. And everything -from the enigmatic characters to the oblique lines to the lingering shots -is a vessel of ambiguity. The film is certain of nothing. And yet Burning manages to get away with saying nothing because it’s easy to mistake the vacuum of meaning for depth. Aestheticised profundity!! Audiences can conjure and project their own meaning into the story because it is cavernous of emotional and thematic substance which creates the falsehood of satisfaction. When a plot is tasked with constructing a vague mystery, it is beholden to leaving enough curiously shaped breadcrumbs to satiate a puzzle-solving  hunger. The trouble I have with this task is its self-serving nature that leaves too little room for a nice dessert, or perhaps a yummy candy :) Something about class divide, somebody's angry dad, a hungry little cat...or a big hungry cat.?..a Porsche....but let's not forget the real sauce of this mystery: a collection of unassuming factoids that are both equally significant and open to interpretation. Chalk up all of the different versions of this movie you can think of, how different are they from each other? and what do each of them have to say about anything? If, within all of these difference, they can be traced back to larger themes that dictate them, what of these larger themes? of manifesting personal reality, dividing people by economic politics, externalizing privilege through destruction? Lee Chang dong's adaption of Murakami is a complete nothingburger. Murakami's whole trick of the cat that may or may not exist, the woman who evaporates mid sentence, the missing thing standing in for a missing meaning has never worked on me. It isn't mystery. It's vagueness borrowing mystery's coat. "Barn Burning," the story underneath this, is itself a riff on Faulkner, and Faulkner actually earned his ambiguity through prose density, through a kid caught between his father's violence and the world's contempt for both of them. Murakami just removes information and calls the hole where it used to be meaning. Lee inherits that hole, dresses it beautifully, and asks us to call it depth. Because nothing major happens here, not really. The entire back half is speculation stacked on speculation, and the film knows it, and dares you to mind. The only saving grace is Yoo Ah in. With him it's a performance you can't look away from.

For much of the runtime, it felt like I was waiting for the thriller elements to begin, and when they finally arrived, the ending came quickly without providing much resolution. In the Burning, Jong-su the main character wants to become a writer, but he almost never writes, his life seems to have a certain emptiness, And he doesn’t seem to really pay much attention or take much agency for most of the movie. Jong su meets a girl he knew from his childhood, Hae mi, and they start spending time together until she leaves for a trip to Africa, and she asks him to watch her cat while she is away. When she returns, she isn’t alone but with a new mysterious friend named Ben. He is apparently wealthy, and his life appears much more put together, a stark contrast compared to Jong Su. After spending some time together with Ben and Hae mi, one evening, Ben reveals his odd hobby to Jong Su. After the reveal of Ben's hobby, the movie starts feeling very sinister and at times eerie. And this reveal sets off a chain of events that consume Jong Su but also for the first time give him a certain meaning, and he starts taking some action but in the process also confusing both Jong Su but also us, the viewers, and with no real explanation to any of them, the movie remains purposefully vague, and it keeps us guessing as to what has really happened and hasn’t happened, keeping the burning truth obscured by smoke. The character of Hae mi plays an important role in translating the message of the movie, and how the characters interact with her might be one of the most important parts of the whole movie. Jong-su appears helpless to the competition from Ben, while maybe also feeling resentment towards him because of their class differences. Hae mi is concerned with her life’s meaning and purpose. Ben and Jong-su are more concerned over who will have “ownership” over her. 4/5

Solid neo-noir that I tried to connect with. I seemed well-equipped to enjoy Burning. I held an affinity for love triangles and mystery, I liked fire motifs, and I also had ample personal lore for the film to mean something to me. However, its impact never hit. Perhaps Burning would’ve had a stronger impact if it focused on Jong-Su and Haemi’s intertwined fates. Facing the same odds in life, the only differing factor was their sex. Unfortunately the film seemed preoccupied with making Haemi’s struggle picturesque and easy to consume. Her hopelessness was unconvincing, not in a way that strengthened the mystery either. She just seemed a little too objectified for my liking. Respectfully, I don’t think weed makes you do all that. When the film was recommended to me, much of the emphasis was on Steven Yeun’s acting. The praise felt contrived; his acting was stellar but the character wasn’t utilised to its full potential for it to be memorable. Burning introduces itself as a Murakami adaptation, but I learnt later that Murakami’s short story was adapted from Faulkner’s work. There’s a rich intertextuality that is missing from my assessment of the film, and I’m inclined to fill that gap. Doing so might distinguish it from Blow-Up, The Long Goodbye, Under the Silver Lake, quietly haunting films about intrigue and ennui. Complaints and praises alike, Burning spurred many subsequent discussions. When asked if the film was more of a window of discovery or a mirror for introspection, I jokingly likened it to a well. Perhaps that’s true. Refreshment and nourishment were there, but somewhat out of reach, drying up even 🫣 And the field of vision was narrow, but one could catch sparse insights if you stared long enough.

I have less to say about Burning than I thought I would. Perhaps I found it too slow or cold. I wanted it to grab me with emotion or mystery or provocation, but for the most part, Burning just simmers. Of course, I think this is the point. I suppose there’s any number of themes available for examination, but I interpreted Burning to be a study in main character syndrome. Lee Jong-su is more or less idled in life. By some combination of his social class and passivity, he is unable to find his footing. So, when Hae-mi (re)enters his frame, and subsequently offers a portal into a life of privilege and agency vis-à-vis Ben, Jong-su spirals. There’s too much ambiguity over the course of the movie for it to be unintentional; yet we watch as Jong-su haphazardly rushes to solve, villainize, and intervene. But it’s too late. In time, it becomes clear that he is leaping to conclusions because the potential for his life to finally develop some meaning is too intoxicating. These ideas are potent, even emotional. For that reason alone, I can recommend Burning with ease. I wish I had loved it, but I’m glad I at least found it great.

NM #287: Final Lee Chang-dong film I watched in preparation for Possible Love (2026) at TIFF, and, once again, this blew me away. This film in particular is one I've been anticipating for quite some time, and it really did not disappoint. Out of every film I've seen from this director, this easily had the most interesting and engaging story out of all of them. The directions this took, and the way all of it was presented was absolutely incredible, and I was completely enamored by it. I loved the characters in this, and the way each of them were performed. Steven Yeun not only gave a career best performance in this, but the performance and character is easily one of my favorites that I've seen from Lee Chang-dong's filmography. The other two leads did a really great job, but Yeun was very clearly the standout. I absolutely loved how the way this character was presented, and how much of him is left up to interpretation. Out of this director's filmography, this might be the most ambiguous film I've seen from him. So much of it is so mysterious, and the little pieces and clues we do find make the actual hidden truth so much more tantalizing. That entire scene between the main character and Steven Yeun at the latter's house in the last act of the movie had some incredible "holy shit" reveals in it. And I love how little of it is actually explained. It's so incredibly thought-provoking and unique. The entire sequence of events here was just nothing short of incredible to watch to watch unfold, and it's one of those things where experiencing it blind really made it so much better. And hoooooo boy was that ending ever satisfying. This film, like Lee Chang-dong's other films is also so impressively shot and directed. There's one scene that takes place between the main trio outside at one of their home's, and the entire thing takes place entirely at dusk, and the level of coordination it must have taken to even capture performances and shots THIS fantastic while also maintaining consistent natural lighting is mind-blowing to me. I genuinely cannot imagine how much of a headache that scene alone was to shoot, but it definitely paid off. The music and sound design was also incredible and worked super well. Anyways, this was yet another absolutely fantastic film from Lee Chang-dong. I'm beyond excited to see his newest at TIFF now, and I'm expecting nothing less than an absolute masterpiece come September 19th (the day I'm actually watching it). 9/10. And in case anyone's curious what my interpretation on the film is, to keep it vague, I personally think that nothing happened to Hae-mi, Ben probably didn't do anything and also lied about *it*, and Jong-su is a misogynistic loser who is possessive over Hae-mi. Honestly, I think this film shares quite a lot thematically with Under the Silver Lake, which is also an amazing film that premiered at Cannes 2018, coincidentally enough.

En 2010, el cineasta coreano Lee Chang-Dong obtuvo en Cannes el premio al Mejor Guion por su filme "Poesía" (Poetry) y desde entonces había guardado silencio. Por eso, su retorno a la edición 2018 del festival francés era esperado con ansiedad por la comunidad cinéfila mundial. Y "Burning" ha estado más que a la altura de las expectativas. Basado en un cuento del reconocido escritor japonés Haruki Murakami, "Burning" es un filme excepcional, realizado con una dirección tan fina como formidable. La historia comienza con el reencuentro en Seúl de dos jóvenes, Jong (Ah In Yoo) y Haemi (Jong-seo Jun) que no se veían desde la infancia que compartieron en el campo. Él, Jong, es un poco tímido y tiene sueños de ser escritor: ella, Haemi, es más desenvuelta y extrovertida. Ambos pasan un rato juntos y Jong queda enganchado. Luego, Haemi se involucra en una relación con Ben (Steven Yeun, conocido por su trabajo en la serie "The Walking Dead"), enigmático millonario que tiene un departamento de lujo y se pasea en un Porsche último modelo. Jong, entretanto, ha regresado a su humilde hogar familiar en el campo, ahora vacío, y mantiene su cercanía con Haemi y confiesa estar enamorado de ella, pero no es correspondido. Viene entonces (al acercarse la mitad de los 168 minutos de metraje) una de esas escenas de antología, que solo los grandes cineastas como Lee Chang-Dong saben filmar. Haemi y su indiferente enamorado Ben deciden visitar a Jong en su casa rural. Jong no los ha invitado pero la pareja se deja caer a toda velocidad en el auto deportivo. La casa está muy cerca de la frontera con Corea del Norte y en la lejanía se escuchan los parlantes de ese país que difunden propaganda hacia los vecinos sureños. Los tres jóvenes conversan un rato y contemplan la puesta de sol. Enseguida Ben saca un pito de marihuana y los tres fuman. Haemi se pone especialmente alegre y se saca la blusa para bailar en topless con el crepúsculo de fondo. Baila al ritmo de la trompeta de Miles Davis en la banda sonora de Ascensor para el cadalso, y el momento que se produce es sublime, al punto que esta puede la mejor de todas las escenas vistas en la competencia del presente festival. El jazz de Miles Davis anuncia el tono sombrío de la segunda mitad del relato, pues la conversación se prolonga mientras llegan las sombras de la noche, momento en que Ben hace una confesión inesperada: le gusta quemar invernaderos. Ese gesto de hacer arder tales construcciones de fierro y plástico –abundantes en el campo surcoreano- es lo único que lo remece de verdad y como él mismo dice, le hace sentir un golpe en el pecho que lo estremece hasta los huesos. En la frialdad cotidiana y distancia emocional de Ben, en la imposibilidad de saber de dónde viene su fortuna, en su tedio constante ante todo lo que no sea la quema de invernaderos, Burning proyecta una lapidaria mirada hacia el sistema capitalista y sus efectos deshumanizadores. Pronto Haemi desparece de la vista de todos y el misterio sobre su paradero provoca que Jong, aún enamorado, emprenda su propia investigación para encontrarla. Con serena maestría, Lee Chang-Dong plantea toda la cinta desde la perspectiva de Jong y es desde allí que el espectador va atando cabos, analizando personalidades, revisando objetos, dándose cuenta de lo que falta. Porque lo que no vemos, lo que no está, lo que la cámara nos escamotea, es esencial en la construcción de este filme que combina la historia de amor con el relato detectivesco. En su manejo virtuoso del fuera de cuadro, el cineasta teje una suerte de teoría cinematográfica del conocimiento. ¿Cuánto podemos llegar a saber de un hecho que nunca vimos? ¿Cuándo podemos decir que es momento de actuar respecto a un suceso sobre el cual no tenemos certeza? "Burning" es un trabajo brillante de dirección de cine y una reflexión filosa sobre la sociedad contemporánea y nuestras limitaciones a la hora de percibir la realidad que nos circunda,

Capolavoro. Mi dispiace averlo visto così tardi, ma meglio adesso che mai. Film capolavoro da tutti i punti di vista. Tra tutti gli aspetti del film, il mio preferito è la sceneggiatura. Lee Chang Dong, almeno per i suoi film che ho visto fin ora (questo e Poetry), ha questo talento nel mettere nel film tanti argomenti, temi o generi insieme, in apparenza in modo disordinato ma aver tutto senso alla fine. Il film inizia come un triangolo amoroso per finire in un mystery. Ed in tutto questo vediamo, oltre al mistero della ragazza, il mistero della giustizia. Come si può vivere in un mondo in cui chi è povero perde e chi è ricco vince sempre. Il caso del padre è rilevante per la storia quanto il mistero della ragazza. A livello politico, è palese quello che dice il film. Viviamo in un mondo in cui ci sono troppi Gatsby. Grandi dialoghi pure nel film. A livello di storia, nonostante sia ispirato a storie di Murakami e Faulkner, è impossibile non pensare ad Antonioni. Il finale ricorda Zabriskie Point, poi la ragazza che scompare è il più classico esempio del cinema del regista italiano. Grande messa in scena. Grande pure la scenografia, che mi ha ricordato Parasite (nonostante sia uscito dopo). Grandi prove attoriali soprattutto nel quanto siano stoici i protagonisti. Steven Yeun fa paura quando dice cose assurde nel modo più normale possibile. Davvero un capolavoro.

cerita perlawanan kelas pekerja terhadap orang kaya yang semena-mena itu selalu berhasil membeli (tidak dalam ruang kapitalisme) saya. belum lagi kini protagonisnya beresonansi dengan saya pribadi yang sama-sama penulis novel yang belum juga debut (bedanya naskah saya sudah diterima dan dalam tahap pengeditan) yang membuat film ini terasa begitu dekat dengan saya pribadi. sebelum masuk ke filmnya sendiri, perlu diketahui saya adalah pembaca sastra jepang yang tidak terlalu suka Haruki Murakami. di novelnya yang berjudul Norwegian Wood, saya sampai harus mencorat-coret satu halaman saking terganggunya dengan adegan seksual yang sebegitu eksplisitnya. bukannya saya anti dengan penggambaran seks dalam konteks sastra, akan tetapi menggambarkannya dengan mentah dan hanya berfokus pada “tata cara mengeluarkan sperma dalam dua halaman” bukanlah sesuatu yang menarik di mata saya. seks seharusnya dapat digambarkan dengan indah dan penuh dinamika kuasa. bisa kok adegan seks itu ditulis dalam rangka menunjukan seberapa telanjang seseorang di hadapan masalah yang ia hadapi atau seberapa kuat seseorang memegang peranan orang lainnya dalam menggerakan cerita. apapun itu, ini dapat diolah menjadi sesuatu yang punya nilai tambah dalam ceritanya itu sendiri. tetapi ya mungkin kebanyakan pembaca suka-suka saja dengan sajian yang seperti ini. di film ini saya tidak menemukan itu. Hae-mi berhasil dibuat sebagai gadis yang menggerakan Jongsu di adegan seks mereka. ada dinamika kuasa yang ditaruh di sana. ditambah bayangan di dinding selagai mereka melakukan itu juga yang memberikan petunjuk tambahan di filmnya sendiri. jadi adegannya tidak serta merta jadi penambah keseksian storytelling Lee Chang-dong. cerita dijalani dengan lamban tetapi tidak membosankan karena selalu ada yang terjadi. kamera dibuat seperti pena yang meliuk, menebar prosa di mana-mana. beberapa dibiarkan tanpa dialog. beberapa kali juga tanpa suara. seru sekali, seperti melihat seorang penyair sedang berpuisi dengan intonasi serta penekanan yang pas. iya, betul. yang pas. bukan yang seperti lomba puisi tingkat kabupaten yang semua pesertanya memakai intonasi yang sama padahal puisinya berkonsep jenaka. kita disuguhkan karakter bernama Ben, seorang kaya yang nggak jelas pekerjaannya apa. kurang lebih seperti orang-orang yang kita sering lihat di pagi hari sedang joging santai dengan kacamata hitam dan earphone di telinganya, ketika kita sendiri sedang berdesak-desakan di dalam transjakarta dengan para pekerja (dan pencari kerja) lainnya. kadang saya berpikir, “mereka kerjanya apa ya?” dan pertanyaan itulah yang ditanyakan Jongsu di awal pertemuan mereka. Haemi di sini ditempatkan sebagai hiburan untuk Ben dan teman-temannya (yang saya yakin bermasalah juga). Sama seperti yang terjadi dewasa ini, di mana kalangan menengah ke bawah disawer di platform digital selama mereka menari-nari tidak jelas di depan kamera ponselnya yang berkabut. di luar tampak seperti berkarya tetapi sejatinya kita memang hanyalah boneka hiburan kala mereka bosan saja. di sinilah yang memberakan Jongsu dengan Haemi. What strikes me the most about Lee Chang-dong's Burning is that throughout its entire 2 hour and 28 minute runtime, nothing happens. This is partly untrue, Burning's second half concedes to some minute thriller conventions but never fully yields to being a standard, by the book thriller. Instead, much of it is this masculine ego war between two men. Two men from completely opposite social classes. The first of these two men is Jong-su, an aspiring writer unable to find employment in Korea's rigidly competitive job market. He's curious and always questions the world around him, and he's very well aware of his class standing. He's aware of the material conditions around him, and he seems to have some sort of knowledge on the issues of capitalism and imperialism (even if this is never outwardly revealed). And standing opposing to him is Ben. Ben is this mysterious figure who stands blissfully ignorant to the world around him. He gets to do so because he's one of the upper elites. And when the inciting incident about halfway into the film occurs, the film becomes a silent battle between the two, attempting to dominate the other, Jong-su channeling his jealousy of Ben's lifestyle while Ben attempts to use his status to elevate himself over Jong-su. However, it is almost impossible to talk about Burning without mentioning the most important character of the film (in my opinion at least), is Hae-Mi. If Jong-su represented the alienation and repressed anger of the lower class Koreans, Hae-Mi serves as an allegory for how women are stripped of their agency under capitalism and its brutal class system. Early on the film, Hae-Mi is introduced to the audience as an old friend of Jong-su, and they go for a dinner together. Here she explains two metaphors, "Little Hunger" and "Great Hunger". "Little Hunger", she says, is the immediate desires of humanity, to fulfill their literal hunger and to survive. However, she then elaborates that the "Great Hunger" is humanity's hunger for meaning in life, some objective truth to the absurdity we live in. Her story is one of the most important parts of the film, yet it is completely depicted through the eyes of Jong-su. It is established that he is completely obsessed over her, yet the film never highlights how much of that love is truly real, or is some infatuation. Through his gaze, she is completely stripped of her agency, mirroring the film's commentary on patriarchy in a Korean society as well. When Hae-Mi dances in the sunset, high on weed and naked from the top, the film drifts into its most hypnotic and stunning. The visuals are truly incredible during this scene, and I was utterly captivated throughout her ritualistic performance. Jong-sus jealousy of her and Ben turned into misogyny and here, as he angrily refers to her as a "whore", the audience begins to see the pent up anger spew out with uncomfortable misogyny, which boils into the final act of the film. Yet, as the end arrived, the film refused to provide any answers. Which is why the ending had more than a few people feel it was futile. There's no final answer, no twist to shock the viewers. Nothing. With this, Lee Chang-dong even questions the genre's conventions of objective finalities, that the final act of violence has any meaning in solving the mystery of the film. The film asserts the mystery isn't the point, the pointlessness IS the point. Whether an objective truth can ever be found is unlikely, all humanity can live on are interpretations of narratives and ideas we build in our heads.
